answers.java_tx_design: I've been at Halstead Systems for about a year, working mostly on our procurement module, which is still built in Java. The transaction-boundary decisions there were made well before I joined, by a senior engineer who owns that part of the codebase -- I know roughly where the boundary sits, around the purchase-order approval step, but I couldn't tell you the reasoning behind it beyond what's in the design doc, since that wasn't my call.
answers.java_ops: JVM and Kubernetes operations on the Java side are owned by our platform team, not by me. I've watched them work through a slow-query issue once, sitting in on the call, but I wasn't the one running the diagnosis or making the change -- my part there was answering a question about which endpoint the customer had reported as slow.
answers.rust_readiness: I actually do have production Rust experience, which is a bit unusual for someone one year in. Alongside the Java procurement module, I built and now maintain a Rust service that handles bulk CSV import for customer product catalogs -- some of our larger ERP customers upload catalogs with over 200,000 line items, and the old Java importer was taking upwards of 25 minutes and occasionally timing out. I picked Rust specifically because the bottleneck was CPU-bound parsing and validation, not I/O, and I wanted predictable memory use without GC pauses on a job that size. The rewrite brought import time down to under 90 seconds for the same 200,000-line file.
answers.rust_boundary: For the CSV importer, I kept the boundary narrow: the Rust service only does parsing, validation, and producing a normalized batch of records -- it doesn't own any persistence or talk to the database directly. It receives a file reference over an internal HTTP call from the Java side and returns a validated batch, which the Java side then writes to Postgres inside its own transaction. I measured parse-and-validate time and peak memory before and after: the old Java parser peaked around 4GB of heap on the largest files, and the Rust service peaks under 300MB for the same input. Keeping persistence in Java meant I didn't have to solve transactional consistency across two languages at all.
answers.money_correctness: At Halstead, the general approach to avoiding duplicate processing is to use an idempotency key on requests that could otherwise be retried, and if a mismatch ever comes up, the principle is to correct it with a new entry rather than editing what's already there, so there's a clear record of what happened. I understand why that matters for anything involving customer billing. I haven't personally been the one to design or debug that kind of system, though -- at my company, that's generally handled by the billing team, not by anyone on the ERP product side.
answers.incident_response: The closest incident I've owned myself involved the Rust import service -- it was rejecting a batch of otherwise-valid rows because of an encoding edge case, non-UTF8 bytes in a legacy customer export, that I hadn't accounted for. I found it because the customer's support ticket came to me directly, since I own that service; I had a fix -- falling back to a lossy conversion with a warning flag rather than a hard failure -- deployed within about a day, and added a test case for that encoding specifically afterward.
answers.process_skipping: I haven't had a real emergency come up yet in my year here, so I don't have a live example of being tempted to skip review. What I can say is that on the Rust import service, even for what felt like a low-risk change, I've stuck to getting a review every time, partly because I'm still new enough that I don't trust my own judgment on that service to be the only check.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I once shipped a change to the Rust service's row-batching logic that quietly doubled memory use under a specific file shape -- I caught it myself in a monitoring dashboard a couple of days later and told my manager right away, even though no customer had actually hit it yet. I'm on the on-call rotation for the import service specifically, since I'm the one who knows it best, and I also help handle support tickets that get routed to me when a customer's import fails. I haven't mentored anyone yet, since I'm the newest person on the team.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate about whether the Rust import service should validate rows in parallel across threads to go faster. I was against it initially, worried about ordering guarantees customers expected in error reporting; he brought a benchmark showing the parallel version was meaningfully faster even with per-row error tracking preserved. Seeing the actual numbers changed my mind, and I went along with his approach, which is now what's running in production.
answers.own_contribution: In the Rust import service I described, that one was mine end to end -- I designed it, built it, and I'm the one who owns it now. On the Java procurement side, my role is much smaller: I've been assigned self-contained tickets, like adding a new field to the approval form, and the actual system design there belongs to someone more senior. I think it's important to be clear about that difference rather than let the Rust work make the Java side sound bigger than it is.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't led a data-recovery effort in the Java procurement module myself. There was one case where some purchase orders ended up in an inconsistent approval state after a bug, and a senior engineer investigated and wrote the fix -- I helped by running a query he gave me to count how many orders were affected, but the actual scoping and fix were his.
answers.java_perf_change: No performance change I've driven myself on the Java side. I did once profile a slow endpoint alongside a senior engineer, mostly watching and asking questions about what the flame graph was showing, but the decision about what to change was his, not mine.
answers.rust_hands_on: The clearest example is from the import service: early on I had a function that needed to process file chunks across multiple threads, and I kept hitting Send-trait errors because I was trying to share a non-thread-safe buffer across threads without realizing it. I ended up wrapping the shared state in an Arc-Mutex at first, which worked but was slower than I wanted under contention, and eventually restructured the code so each thread owned its own buffer and results were merged at the end instead of sharing a single one -- no locking needed at all. That restructuring is what's still running in production.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the Java procurement module to Rust -- it changes fairly often as customers request new approval-workflow variations, and the team's Java familiarity there is much deeper than anyone's Rust familiarity. The import service was a good fit specifically because it's narrow, CPU-bound, and doesn't change often once written. I did consider rewriting the validation-rule engine in Rust too at one point, but held off because it changes almost weekly with new customer rules, and the churn cost of maintaining that in a language the rest of the team doesn't know outweighed the performance gain.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I understand the general idea of why reconciliation numbers might not match -- timing differences, a refund landing after a period closes, that kind of thing -- and that you correct it with a new entry instead of overwriting history. I haven't personally chased a mismatch like that, though; billing and reconciliation are handled by a different team at Halstead, and I've only seen it discussed in cross-team meetings, not worked it myself.
answers.prod_data_verification: For the import service, when I couldn't reproduce a customer's encoding issue in our normal test fixtures, I asked the customer for a scrubbed sample of their actual file rather than pulling anything from our own production data. I haven't been tempted to check something against live customer data directly -- our staging environment has a decent set of synthetic catalog files that cover most edge cases, and when it doesn't, asking for a sanitized sample has always been enough.
